title: Inference load patterns and repeatability checks
body:
Purpose:
Quick reference for constructing throughput benchmark experiments that emphasize repeatability across runs and produce actionable bottleneck signals. This is a working doc — notes-to-self + checklist + concrete load-config snippets we can copy into experiments.

Scope:
- Focus: inference throughput experiments (tokens/sec and requests/sec), end-to-end through runtime to GPU.
- Not covering: long-running stateful workloads, distributed multi-node training.

High-level goals (what "good" looks like):
- Reproducible within noise budget: long-run coefficient of variation (CV) for throughput <= 3% across at least 3 independent repeats.
- Stable measurement window: percentiles (p50/p95/p99) converge and tail shapes are consistent across repeats.
- Clear bottleneck signals: GPU utilization, host CPU, PCIe, or scheduling gaps show consistent correlated behavior with throughput drops.

Quick checklist before any run:
- [ ] Pin model variant + tokenization + sequence length distribution.
- [ ] Fix random seeds where applicable (sampling/beam).
- [ ] Ensure no concurrent noisy jobs on same host (night/weekend lab runs are easiest).
- [ ] Snapshot serving binary + container image digest + kernel version.
- [ ] Record runtime config: batcher settings, max-batch-latency-ms, batching strategy, micro-batch size, KV cache mode.
- [ ] Start metrics exporters (Prom, DCGM) and perf traces.
- [ ] Warmup sequence complete and validated (see warmup section).

Load injection patterns (templates):
1) Steady-state constant RPS/throughput
   - Purpose: baseline steady throughput and tail stability
   - Pattern: hold constant arrival rate for N minutes (examples: 5m, 15m, 60m)
   - Useful for capacity and batching efficiency measurements

2) Linear ramp
   - Purpose: find knee of throughput and autoscaler behavior
   - Pattern: ramp RPS from low->high over T minutes, then hold
   - Example: 0 -> 1000 req/s over 10m, then hold at 1000 req/s for 15m

3) Bursty/sawtooth (periodic spikes)
   - Purpose: stress transient scheduling, cold-batching overheads, autoscale response
   - Pattern: cyclical spikes (10s spike every 2m) or Poisson bursts

4) Poisson/chaotic arrivals
   - Purpose: realistic client traffic; evaluates jitter and batching randomness

5) KV-prefill + hot-prefix sequence
   - Purpose: measure benefit of KV cache; run a phase of prefix traffic to populate cache then measure throughput on hot requests

Warmup sequences (recommended three-phase):
- Phase A — Priming (2–5 minutes): low-rate requests that exercise model initialization, upload tokenizer caches, warm JIT kernels if applicable. Goal: ensure file caches and model weights are resident, first GPU kernels compiled.
- Phase B — Batch ramp (5–10 minutes): gradually increase RPS to target while using same request distribution. This surfaces any dynamic compilation or initial scheduling adjustments.
- Phase C — Steady pre-measure (5–15 minutes): hold at target load to let batching behavior and KV cache reach steady state before starting measurements. Only after Phase C start measurement window.

Repeatability protocol:
- Minimum repeats: 3 independent runs per experiment (prefer 5 for production claims).
- Isolation: stop all non-test services on node(s); pin CPU governor; set network QoS if possible.
- Determinism knobs: seeds, fixed tokenizer version, deterministic allocator if offered by runtime.
- Run spacing: allow a cool-down (2–5 minutes) or full container restart between repeats to avoid residual caching effects unless testing cache persistence.
- Reported statistics: per-run median throughput, p50/p95/p99 latencies, token/sec, GPU utilization (avg and std), CPU steal, and NVMe/PCIe counters.
- Statistical checks: compute CV across run medians; bootstrap CI for median and p95. If CV > 5%, investigate noise sources before drawing conclusions.

Noise sources & mitigations:
- Background OS jitter: use dedicated test nodes + cpuset isolation, disable turbo/CPU frequency scaling where feasible.
- Network jitter: colocate loadgen or use high-bandwidth NICs; measure RTT variance.
- NVMe activity: ensure no background writes; use ephemeral instance storage or provisioned IOPS.
- Thermal throttling: monitor package temperature; prefer lab machines with stable cooling.
- GPU scheduler preemption: track other GPU users; use GPU exclusivity for tests.

Metrics to collect (minimum):
- Inference metrics: requests/sec, tokens/sec, per-request token count, batch-size distribution, batch latency distribution, queue times.
- Host/GPU: nvidia-smi utilization, sm_util, gpu_memory_usage, pcie_tx/rx, host_cpu%, iowait, irq.
- Runtime internals: batcher queue length over time, batch assembly latency, KV cache hit/miss rates, micro-batch count, kernel compilation events.
- Traces: end-to-end request trace IDs to correlate drops with spikes in queue length or kernel stalls.

Instrumentation tips:
- Emit a short JSON payload per request with a correlation_id and epoch timestamp for trace alignment.
- Add a lightweight runtime metric for "batch_assemble_duration_ms" and record histogram.
- Use Prom exporter with 15s scrape during warmup; increase resolution to 5s for measurement window if possible.

Example loadgen snippets (we use vegeta or an internal harness):
- Vegeta target (approx):
  {
    "method": "POST",
    "url": "http://localhost:8080/v1/generate",
    "body": "{\"input\":\"translate: Hello world\"}",
    "header": {"Content-Type": "application/json"}
  }
  Command: vegeta attack -duration=15m -rate=500 -targets=targets.json | vegeta report -type=json > vegeta-run-1.json

- k6 JS ramp example (sketch):
  export let options = { stages: [ { duration: '5m', target: 0 }, { duration: '10m', target: 500 }, { duration: '15m', target: 500 } ] }
  // call runtime endpoint, include correlation id header

Internal harness flags (copyable):
  --config batcher.max_latency_ms=20 --config batcher.max_batch_size=32 --loadgen.sequence_distribution=chat-multiturn --random-seed=42 --kv-prefill=true --metrics-interval=5s

Measurement window guidelines:
- Warmup phases done, then measure for at least 15 minutes for steady-state workloads.
- For bursty tests, measure across multiple cycles (>=5 cycles) to capture variance.

Acceptance criteria example (draft):
- Throughput CV across runs < 3% AND
- p95 tail shape reproducible (visual check) AND
- At least one clear correlated resource signal when throttling occurs (e.g., GPU SM saturation or batching queue growth).

Troubleshooting playbook (quick):
1) High variance in runs: check background processes, CPU steal, scrape intervals.
2) Throughput lower than expected but GPU idle: inspect batcher queue length and max_batch_size config.
3) Short, frequent latency spikes: check kernel compile events, JITing or cold kernel paths.
4) Sharp drops at certain RPS: investigate PCIe / NVLink saturation and host network limits.

Experiment template (copy into issue):
- experiment_id: <short id>
- model: <name + version + quantization>
- node: <instance/id>
- config_flags: <key=value,...>
- load_pattern: <steady|ramp|burst> + params
- warmup: <phases durations>
- repeats: 3
- results_blob: <s3 or artifact link>
- notes: <observations>

Open questions / follow-ups:
- How to standardize warmup duration per-model? heuristic: scale by model size (tokens/sec to fill KV cache) — need to validate.
- Should we always restart container between repeats or allow re-used cache for production-like persistence experiments?
- Investigate automated detection for "insufficient warmup" by looking at trend slope in throughput during pre-measure phase.

References / prior runs:
- linked_artifacts: CONFLUENCE-12345 (experiment log), JIRA-RT-998 (bug tracking noisy runs), PR #42 loadgen harness changes.

Notes-to-self:
- When in doubt, run longer measurement windows rather than shorter.
- Keep a canonical script in the repo that executes exact reproduce steps for any published benchmark.
- Capture a snapshot of nvidia-smi top output every 10s during runs — super helpful for correlating micro spikes.

End of doc.
